intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns where reviewers slip. Work the section exercises in pencil, check yourself with the recall questions, and write your own protocol beside mine as you go.

sections.title: Why Synthesis, and What Kind
sections.big_idea: A review is **a study of studies**. It reads everything on a question by stated rules, so another team can repeat the search and reach the same set.
in_plain_words: An ordinary literature review reflects what its author happened to read. Two authors on one topic produce two reading lists and cannot say why they differ. A systematic review records its search, states its criteria in advance and applies the same appraisal to every study, so a reader can re-run it and see where each study went.

Reviews come in a family, and **the question picks the member**. Effect questions (works, reduces, increases) go to a systematic review. 'What is known' questions go to scoping or a gap map. 'Why' and 'under what conditions' questions need realist synthesis. Settle this before you agree a timeline.

diagram.caption: the question's verb chooses the review

key_terms.meaning: Explicit, pre-specified, reproducible methods to find, select, appraise and synthesise all relevant research.
A review written from what the author knows and can find, with invisible selection.
Maps what has been studied and where the gaps are, without appraising or synthesising effects.
Asks what works for whom, in what circumstances and why.
A grid of interventions and outcomes showing where studies exist and where cells are blank.
A public list of review protocols run by the University of York.

worked_example.title: Which review fits?
worked_example.setup: A programme officer brings you four questions and asks which kind of review each one needs.
steps: 'Does conditional cash transfer raise secondary enrolment?' The verb raises makes it an effect question, so a systematic review.
'What is known about self-help groups and women's political participation?' This asks what has been studied, so a scoping review or gap map.
'Why did community health worker schemes work in Chhattisgarh and stall elsewhere?' The word why points to realist synthesis.
'How do adolescent girls experience menstrual health programmes?' This asks about experience, so qualitative evidence synthesis.
worked_example.answer: Systematic review, scoping review or gap map, realist synthesis, qualitative evidence synthesis.

mistakes: Paying for a systematic-review timeline when the question is really a scoping one, or the reverse.
Reading a review with invisible selection as if it were systematic because it has many references.
Assuming a review of a global literature is a review of India. Most reviews that touch India are not Indian reviews.
Quoting one landmark trial as settled when the pooled trials say something different.

recall.q: What is the unit of observation in a systematic review?
recall.a: The study; a person is never the unit.

recall.q: Which review type suits a question with the verb 'reduces'?
recall.a: A systematic review, with meta-analysis if the studies are similar.

recall.q: Name two cases in the deck where the body of studies disagreed with the famous study.
recall.a: Deworming and microfinance.

recall.q: Where should you start for a South Asian development question?
recall.a: The 3ie portal and Campbell's international development group, then Cochrane for health outcomes.

recall.q: What does the deck say is the most common error in commissioned reviews?
recall.a: Asking a scoping question and paying for a systematic-review timeline, or the reverse.

sections.title: The Question and the Protocol
sections.big_idea: Fix **the question, the criteria and the plan** before searching. Then file them publicly, so changes after the fact are visible.
in_plain_words: PICO splits a question into population, intervention, comparison and outcome. Adding study design gives PICOS and decides whether only randomised trials count. Write the eligibility criteria as sentences a screener could apply without asking you. 'Studies of women's empowerment' is too vague to apply; a list of named measures for a stated age group is not.

Aim for a question that returns roughly ten to a few hundred eligible studies. The protocol records the question, sources, search, screening, extraction, risk-of-bias tool, synthesis plan and reporting standard. **Record it publicly before you search**, on PROSPERO for health outcomes or OSF for the rest, and staff the review with at least two people.

key_terms.meaning: Population, intervention, comparison, outcome: the four parts of a review question.
Inclusion and exclusion rules written as sentences a screener can apply.
The written plan for the whole review, fixed before the search.
The 17-item checklist for review protocols.
A free, public, time-stamped entry of the protocol, as on PROSPERO.
Quiet change of outcomes or criteria after seeing the studies.

worked_example.title: Turn a vague aim into criteria
worked_example.setup: A colleague wants a review of 'women's empowerment' programmes and has written only that phrase.
steps: Population: fix it. Adult women in low- and middle-income countries in group-based savings or credit programmes.
Comparison: no programme, or waitlist.
Outcomes: name them. Economic, social and political measures such as decision-making index, mobility and control over earnings.
Designs: RCT, or quasi-experimental with a comparison group.
Test each line: could a screener apply it without asking you?
worked_example.answer: Each criterion becomes a sentence a screener can apply, and the protocol can be registered.

mistakes: Writing criteria such as 'studies of women's empowerment' that two screeners will read differently.
Changing criteria after seeing the results to admit a study you like, which is moving the goalposts.
Skipping the second screener on a doctoral review instead of arranging a sample check and reporting the disagreement rate.
Deciding subgroups after seeing the results, so a reader cannot tell a finding from a fishing trip.

recall.q: What does the S in PICOS add?
recall.a: Study design, which decides whether only randomised trials count.

recall.q: Why file a protocol publicly?
recall.a: It stops duplication and it stops drift, since the registered version is what the published methods are compared with.

recall.q: What is the mean time from registration to publication reported by Borah and colleagues?
recall.a: 67 weeks across 195 reviews.

recall.q: What is the minimum review team on the deck's table?
recall.a: A lead reviewer and a second independent screener and extractor, with a librarian, even for a day.

recall.q: When does the deck suggest OSF Registries?
recall.a: For reviews outside health, such as education, livelihoods and governance.

sections.title: Searching
sections.big_idea: The search decides the evidence base. Use **several databases, grey literature and citation chasing**, and log every step.
in_plain_words: No single database finds every study: in Bramer's tests, four databases together recalled 98 per cent. Build the string one concept at a time, joining synonyms with OR inside a block and blocks with AND. Use controlled vocabulary such as MeSH next to free text, and test the string against studies you already know.

Development evidence lives outside journals. Search donor and NGO sites, theses on Shodhganga and regional institutes, then use citation chasing, hand-searching and emails. **Log each search as you run it**: database, date, string, limits and record count. Export in full to a reference manager and deduplicate before screening.

diagram.note: run it in each database, with its own tags and thesaurus

key_terms.meaning: Synonyms joined by OR within a concept, concepts joined by AND.
Catches plurals and variants: school* finds school, schools and schooling.
The controlled vocabulary used to tag records in MEDLINE.
Evaluations and reports published outside journals, such as donor or NGO PDFs.
Reading reference lists backwards and finding citing studies forwards.
A record of each search with database, date, string, limits and record count.

worked_example.title: Build a string for self-help groups
worked_example.setup: You want studies of self-help group programmes and women's decision-making.
steps: Intervention block: "self-help group*" OR SHG, joined by OR.
Population block: women OR female.
Outcome block: "decision-making" OR mobility OR "control over earnings". Drop it if outcomes are named inconsistently.
Join the blocks with AND, and limit to title, abstract and keywords with TITLE-ABS-KEY in Scopus.
Test against five studies you already know. If one is missing, edit the string.
worked_example.answer: A three-block string, tested against known studies and logged with database, date and record count.

mistakes: Relying on Google Scholar alone. It caps results, ranks opaquely and cannot be reproduced.
Searching the outcome too tightly, so studies that report it only as a secondary result never surface.
Forgetting to log grey searches, which PRISMA-S wants site by site with dates and terms.
Concluding South Asian evidence is thin when the regional sources were never searched. It is thinly indexed.

recall.q: How many databases does the deck say to plan for at minimum?
recall.a: At least three, plus the field-specific ones.

recall.q: What does Boolean OR do inside a block?
recall.a: It joins synonyms for one concept.

recall.q: Why is Shodhganga useful?
recall.a: It holds Indian doctoral theses in full text, evidence nobody else indexes.

recall.q: How many Google Scholar results does the convention screen?
recall.a: The first 200 to 300, with the cut-off reported.

recall.q: What should you do with duplicates before screening?
recall.a: Remove them and record how many, since PRISMA asks.

sections.title: Screening and Selection
sections.big_idea: Two people screen **every record against written criteria**, and every record is accounted for in a flow diagram that adds up.
in_plain_words: Screening runs in two stages. At title and abstract the rule is when in doubt, keep. At full text each exclusion gets a reason from a fixed list. Two screeners work independently, a pilot on 100 records tests the criteria, and the agreement is reported as kappa. Single screeners miss a median of 13 per cent of eligible records.

Tools such as Rayyan blind the screeners and count what PRISMA asks for. Machine ranking can speed the work but a person still reads every record shown, and a stopping rule must be stated. **The PRISMA flow diagram is the first thing a methodologist checks**, so make its arithmetic exact.

diagram.caption: illustrative counts from the deck's flow diagram

key_terms.meaning: Two people judge every record independently, then resolve conflicts.
Agreement between raters corrected for chance; above 0.6 reads as substantial.
Both screeners take the same 100 records and discuss every disagreement.
The stated point at which prioritised screening ends.
A fixed-list reason given for each full-text exclusion.
One study can have several reports; PRISMA counts both.

worked_example.title: Check the flow diagram adds up
worked_example.setup: A review reports 4,212 database records and 318 from other sources, with 1,140 duplicates removed. Illustrative counts.
steps: Total identified: 4,212 + 318 = 4,530.
After duplicates: 4,530 − 1,140 = 3,390 screened.
Excluded at title and abstract: 3,102, so sought: 3,390 − 3,102 = 288.
Not retrieved: 9, so assessed: 288 − 9 = 279.
Excluded at full text: 238, so included reports: 279 − 238 = 41.

mistakes: Using one screener to save weeks. The saved time is bought with missed studies and an indefensible review.
Excluding a study at full text without a recorded reason from the fixed list.
Writing 'we used ASReview' and nothing about the stopping rule.
Counting papers as studies, so one trial with three reports appears three times.

recall.q: What is the rule at title and abstract stage?
recall.a: When in doubt, keep the record.

recall.q: What kappa is conventionally substantial?
recall.a: Above 0.6.

recall.q: What did Waffenschmidt and colleagues find about single screeners?
recall.a: They missed a median of 13 per cent of eligible records.

recall.q: What is Rayyan's blind mode for?
recall.a: So neither screener sees the other's votes until conflicts are resolved.

recall.q: Why budget screening in hours?
recall.a: A tight deadline can then be recognised as a request for a rapid review.

sections.title: Data Extraction
sections.big_idea: Design the form from the protocol, **pilot it, and extract twice**. The form decides what the review can answer.
in_plain_words: Extraction turns 40 papers into one table. Write the form before you open a paper, include a page-and-table source for every number, and pilot it on five studies with two extractors. Capture the forgettable items: the comparator, the unit of assignment and the timepoints.

Papers rarely report the number you need, so convert from what they give, and record the route. Watch three complications: shared control groups, several reports of one study, and cluster designs analysed as individuals. Ask authors for specific missing numbers, derive when you can, impute last, and **test whether the result changes**.

diagram.caption: groups of items every form needs

key_terms.meaning: The piloted template that records one row per study.
1 + (m − 1)ρ, used to inflate standard errors of cluster trials.
Intra-cluster correlation, taken from the paper or a similar study.
Standardised mean difference, used to combine different scales.
Two people extract each outcome, the Cochrane minimum for numerical data.
Borrowing a value such as an SD from similar studies, then testing the effect.

worked_example.title: Two conversions and a design effect
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A trial reports a mean and SE with 100 participants, another a 95% CI with 49 participants, and a third is clustered.
steps: SD from SE: SD = SE × √n, so with SE 2.0 and n = 100 (√n = 10): 2.0 × 10 = 20.
SD from CI with n = 49 (√n = 7), CI 4.0 to 12.0: 7 × 8 = 56.
Design effect with m = 21 and ρ = 0.05: (21 − 1) × 0.05 = 1.
Then add one: 1 + 1 = 2.
worked_example.answer: SDs of 20 and 14.29, and a design effect of 2 for the clustered trial.

mistakes: Adding a field after twenty papers, which means going back through all twenty.
Extracting only the p-value, which gives no effect size.
Pooling two treatment arms against the same control as if they were independent.
Reading 'not reported' as 'no effect' instead of recording it as a risk-of-bias signal.

recall.q: Why pilot the form on five studies?
recall.a: Disagreements show whether the form or the paper is ambiguous, before the rest is extracted.

recall.q: What did Buscemi and colleagues find about single extraction?
recall.a: 21.7 per cent more errors than double extraction, at 36.1 per cent less time.

recall.q: What are the three responses to missing data, in order?
recall.a: Ask, derive, impute.

recall.q: How should a cluster trial analysed at individual level be handled?
recall.a: Inflate its standard errors by the design effect and say which ICC you used.

recall.q: Which rows do people forget on a form?
recall.a: The comparator, the unit of assignment and the timepoints.

sections.title: Risk of Bias and Study Quality
sections.big_idea: Judge each study **by outcome and by area of design**, never by a summed score, and let the judgement change the synthesis.
in_plain_words: Risk of bias asks whether a study's design or conduct could have produced a systematic error. RoB 2 covers randomised trials in five areas, ROBINS-I covers non-randomised studies starting with confounding, and a 3ie and Campbell tool covers difference-in-differences, matching, IV and RDD by their identifying assumptions. Other designs have their own tools.

Then deal with the studies you did not find. Publication bias means significant results are more likely to be written up, so prevent it by searching registries and theses and detect it with funnel plots when you have at least ten studies. **Use the appraisal in the table, the sensitivity analysis, GRADE and the discussion**, or it is decoration.

key_terms.meaning: Likelihood that design or conduct produced a systematic error in the estimate.
Cochrane tool for randomised trials, with five areas and three judgements.
Tool for non-randomised studies; judgements run low to critical.
Effect against precision; a missing corner can hint at publication bias.
Regression test for funnel asymmetry; meaningless below ten studies.
Imputes missing mirror-image studies; treat it as a sensitivity analysis only.

worked_example.title: Overall RoB 2 judgement and the file drawer
worked_example.setup: A trial scores low, some concerns, high, low, low across the five RoB 2 areas. Separately, Franco found 10 of 48 null studies and 56 of 91 strong studies published.
steps: The overall judgement is the worst area, which is high.
So this trial is at high risk for that outcome.
Share of null studies published: 10 ÷ 48 = 0.21.
Share of strong studies published: 56 ÷ 91 = 0.62.
worked_example.answer: High risk overall; about 21 per cent of null results against 62 per cent of strong results were published.

mistakes: Summing points into a quality score. Cochrane advises against any total score.
Reporting a careful appraisal table and then treating every study alike in the synthesis.
Drawing a funnel plot for six studies and declaring no evidence of publication bias.
Calling funnel asymmetry publication bias without considering real heterogeneity.

recall.q: How many areas does RoB 2 judge and what are the three judgements?
recall.a: Five areas; low risk, some concerns, high risk.

recall.q: Which area comes first in ROBINS-I?
recall.a: Confounding.

recall.q: Name two checks for a difference-in-differences study.
recall.a: Evidence for parallel pre-trends and enough pre-periods to see them.

recall.q: What is the minimum number of studies for Egger's test or a funnel plot?
recall.a: Ten.

recall.q: Name the three later steps the risk-of-bias judgement must feed.
recall.a: Sensitivity analysis, GRADE and the discussion.

sections.title: Meta-Analysis
sections.big_idea: A pooled estimate is **a weighted average where precision sets the weight**. Report how much the studies disagree as well as the average.
in_plain_words: Meta-analysis combines effect estimates, weighting each by the inverse of its variance. First choose a common measure, then a model. Fixed effect assumes one true effect, while random effects assumes a distribution and is the default in development because programmes vary by site and implementer.

Report Q, I², τ² and a prediction interval, and explain heterogeneity with pre-specified subgroups or meta-regression. Count studies and effect sizes separately, and run sensitivity checks including leave-one-out. In the deck's example the fixed-effect interval excluded zero and the random-effects interval did not, so **the model choice changed the conclusion**.

diagram.note: weight w = 1 ÷ SE², so precise studies count more

key_terms.meaning: Weight of a study, 1 ÷ SE²; precise studies count for more.
Assumes one common true effect; studies differ only by sampling error.
Assumes a distribution of true effects and adds τ² to every variance.
Share of observed variation beyond chance, a proportion not an amount.
Where a new study's effect would likely fall.
Variance estimation allowing many effects per study, clustered by study.

worked_example.title: Pool three studies, fixed effect
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. Study A has effect 0.20 and SE 0.10, B has 0.35 and 0.20, C has 0.05 and 0.05.
steps: Weights are 1 ÷ SE²: 100, 25 and 400, so the sum is 100 + 25 + 400 = 525.
A's weight times effect: 100 × 0.20 = 20.
Pooled effect: 48.75 ÷ 525 = 0.093.
worked_example.answer: Pooled effect 0.093. Study C carries about three-quarters of the weight.

mistakes: Pooling across effect measures without converting everything to one metric first.
Reading I² as a verdict instead of reporting τ² and a prediction interval.
Letting one paper contribute twelve effect sizes as twelve independent studies.
Testing ten post-hoc subgroups and reporting the one that came out significant.

recall.q: What decides a study's weight in a fixed-effect meta-analysis?
recall.a: Its precision, 1 divided by SE squared.

recall.q: What does τ² measure?
recall.a: The between-study variance in effect-size units.

recall.q: Why is random effects the default in development?
recall.a: Programmes differ by site, implementer and comparator.

recall.q: How many studies per moderator does Cochrane's rule of thumb require in meta-regression?
recall.a: At least ten.

recall.q: What does leave-one-out do?
recall.a: Re-runs the analysis k times, dropping each study, to find studies whose removal changes the conclusion.

sections.title: Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis
sections.big_idea: When you cannot pool, synthesise **by a stated method**: count directions, structure the text or build a realist account, and report to SWiM.
in_plain_words: Incompatible scales, different programmes under one name or missing statistics can rule out pooling. The SWiM guideline asks you to group studies by a logic stated in advance, standardise effects where possible and tabulate them. Counting directions of effect, tested with a sign test, is better than counting significant results, though it never says how big the effect is.

Qualitative evidence has its own methods: thematic, framework, meta-ethnography, realist and meta-aggregation, rated with CERQual. Realist reviews ask what works for whom and why, mixed-methods reviews join the two streams in a matrix, and scoping reviews and gap maps chart what exists. **Pick the method from the question** and report it fully.

key_terms.meaning: Synthesis Without Meta-analysis: a nine-item reporting guideline.
Counting studies by direction of effect, tested with a sign test.
One bar per study, placed by direction, height by quality.
A tool to rate confidence in qualitative review findings.
A context-mechanism-outcome statement.
Grid of interventions and outcomes showing what evidence exists.

worked_example.title: Count directions of effect
worked_example.setup: Ten studies of one programme. Four are significant and positive, four are positive but not significant, two point the wrong way. Illustrative.
steps: Count by significance: 4 of 10 studies. That sounds like 'mostly fails'.
Count by direction: 4 + 4 = 8 positive.
Compare with the deck's reference rows: 9 of 10 gives p = 0.02 and 6 of 10 gives p = 0.75. Eight sits between them.
Report the count with its denominator and the risk of bias.
worked_example.answer: 8 of 10 studies point in a positive direction, which says nothing yet about size.

mistakes: Writing 'most studies found a positive effect' without how many, out of how many and at what risk of bias.
Counting significant studies, which makes a true small effect look absent when studies are underpowered.
Using 'mechanism' for any intermediate step in a realist review.
Forgetting that a realist review does not produce an effect size.

recall.q: What does SWiM stand for?
recall.a: Synthesis Without Meta-analysis.

recall.q: Why count directions and not significance?
recall.a: Underpowered studies of a true effect often miss significance, so the count says it does not work.

recall.q: Which qualitative method starts from an a priori framework?
recall.a: Framework synthesis.

recall.q: What did Evans and Popova find about six reviews of learning?
recall.a: Only 3 of 227 studies appeared in all six.

recall.q: What does a scoping review leave out?
recall.a: Appraisal of bias and synthesis of effects.

sections.title: GRADE and Reporting
sections.big_idea: GRADE gives **a certainty rating per outcome**, and PRISMA 2020 makes the review checkable. Write the abstract's verbs to match the rating.
in_plain_words: GRADE rates certainty as high, moderate, low or very low for each outcome. Randomised evidence starts high and observational evidence starts low. You downgrade for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias, each by one level or two, and upgrade observational evidence in three situations. Record a written reason for every judgement.

A summary-of-findings table shows effects in absolute terms at a stated baseline, with certainty beside each outcome. Report to PRISMA 2020 and fill the checklist against your own draft. The discussion keeps limits of evidence apart from limits of the review, and the applicability paragraph says what transfers. **Plan the update** and put the search date on page one.

diagram.caption: five reasons move evidence down, three move it up

key_terms.meaning: Confidence that the estimate is close to the true effect, per outcome.
Lower the rating by one or two levels for each of five reasons.
A sample benchmark; totals below it can justify an imprecision downgrade.
One-page table of key outcomes in absolute terms with certainty ratings.
A 27-item reporting checklist with a flow diagram.
A review that re-runs the search at set intervals and publishes the current version.

worked_example.title: From a relative effect to a sentence
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. Seven RCTs find a risk ratio for enrolment of 1.08 (1.04 to 1.12) from a baseline of 75 per 100.
steps: Expected enrolment with the programme: 75 × 1.08 = 81 per 100.
Absolute effect: 81 − 75 = 6 more per 100.
Lower bound: 75 × 1.04 = 78, so 78 − 75 = 3 more.
Upper bound: 75 × 1.12 = 84, so 84 − 75 = 9 more.
Add the certainty: moderate, downgraded for inconsistency.
worked_example.answer: Cash transfers probably increase enrolment, by about 6 per 100 (3 to 9 more), with moderate certainty.

mistakes: Quoting a relative effect with no baseline, which means different things at 20 and 95 per cent.
Writing 'improves' in the abstract above a low rating.
Mixing limits of the evidence with limits of your own search and screening.
Ending with 'more research is needed' in place of a specific, fundable study.

recall.q: What are the four GRADE certainty levels?
recall.a: High, moderate, low and very low.

recall.q: Name the five reasons to downgrade.
recall.a: Risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias.

recall.q: How many items does PRISMA 2020 have?
What does PRISMA item 7 ask for?
recall.a: The full search strategy for every database, verbatim, as run.

recall.q: How soon does the median review need updating, per Shojania?
recall.a: About five and a half years.

sections.title: Bibliometric Analysis
sections.big_idea: Bibliometrics maps **who publishes what and how it connects**. It describes a field and cannot say what works.
in_plain_words: A bibliometric analysis counts thousands of records and reads none, so it maps structure. Performance analysis counts authors, journals and citations. Science mapping builds networks using co-citation, bibliographic coupling, co-authorship and keyword co-occurrence. Pick the source first, since Scopus and Web of Science under-represent regional and non-English work.

Cleaning takes half the time, the maps need clusters named by reading their central papers, and indicators such as the h-index and impact factor are easily misused. Report output and uptake separately, check for predatory journals and save every file. **Pair the analysis with another product** and never present it as a review.

key_terms.meaning: Quantitative study of publications and their citation and authorship links.
Two documents cited together; shows the intellectual structure.
Two documents sharing references; shows the current research front.
h papers with at least h citations each.
A core of few journals holds a third of the papers on a topic.
Authors producing n papers fall roughly as 1 over n squared.

worked_example.title: Work out an h-index
worked_example.setup: An author's six papers have 25, 12, 7, 4, 3 and 1 citations. Illustrative.
steps: Rank the papers from most to least cited.
Test each rank: does paper number h have at least h citations?
Paper 4 has 4 citations, which is at least 4, so h is at least 4.
Paper 5 has 3 citations, which is under 5, so h is not 5.
Remember the limits: the h-index only rises and rewards volume.

mistakes: Calling a citation count a literature review, or reporting PRISMA for a bibliometric analysis.
Concluding that the most-cited intervention works. Citation measures attention.
Running the study on Web of Science alone and missing Indian, Bangladeshi and Nepali journals.
Describing every default figure in a paragraph and ending with 'the field is growing'.

recall.q: Which technique shows the current research front?
recall.a: Bibliographic coupling.

recall.q: What does co-citation analysis show?
recall.a: The intellectual structure, with clusters of foundational works.

recall.q: Which step takes about half the time in a bibliometric workflow?
recall.a: Cleaning the data.

recall.q: What does the Leiden Manifesto's first principle say?
recall.a: Quantitative evaluation should support expert judgement and never replace it.

recall.q: Name two checks before counting a journal.
recall.a: Any two of DOAJ, the Scopus source list, COPE membership, Think Check Submit.

sections.title: Practice, Tools and Pitfalls
sections.big_idea: A full review is possible **on free tools with a small team**, if you protect the second screener and the librarian.
in_plain_words: A free stack covers every stage: registries for protocols, free and institutional databases for search, Zotero, Rayyan, spreadsheets, the Cochrane risk-of-bias tools, R or Jamovi, GRADEpro and the PRISMA flow-diagram generator. A realistic timeline is 26 to 46 weeks of effort across four to six part-time people.

AI tools may draft strings and give a first extraction pass, but they must be measured and disclosed. Twelve pitfalls recur, and the six-box reading routine lets you test any published review in twenty minutes. **Check the abstract's verbs against the certainty rating**, and write the applicability paragraph for South Asia.

diagram.caption: typical effort, 26 to 46 weeks in all

key_terms.meaning: A set of free tools covering every stage of a review.
A 16-item tool for appraising reviews, seven items critical.
A review compressed to 8–12 weeks by restricting sources, dates and extraction.
Share of eligible records an AI screener finds; below about 95% it cannot exclude.
A paragraph saying what in the evidence transfers to your setting.
A recurring error, each with a prevention on the deck's table.

worked_example.title: Read a review in six boxes
worked_example.setup: You are handed a review whose abstract says 'cash transfers improve learning'. Use the deck's six boxes.
steps: Registration: is there a protocol, and does the paper match it?
Search: which databases and date, and is the strategy in an appendix?
Flow: do the numbers add up, with exclusions listed with reasons?
Appraisal: which tool, how many people, and was it used in the synthesis?
Synthesis: pooled or narrative, which model, and how was heterogeneity reported?
Certainty: if GRADE says low, the abstract should say 'may'.
worked_example.answer: A low-certainty rating with 'improve' in the abstract is a mismatch to flag.

mistakes: Skipping the librarian and the second screener, the two roles that cannot be recovered later.
Using an AI discovery tool as the only search, which fails PRISMA item 7.
Promising a living review with no budget line.
Applying evidence from Latin America to Nepal without a paragraph on transfer.

recall.q: Which tool produces the summary-of-findings table?
recall.a: GRADEpro GDT, free for non-commercial use.

recall.q: What is the total typical effort in weeks on the deck's table?
recall.a: 26 to 46 weeks.

recall.q: What should you report about an AI tool you used?
recall.a: The tool, version, date, prompt, purpose and how output was checked.

recall.q: How many items does AMSTAR 2 have and how many are critical?
recall.a: 16 items, seven of them critical.

recall.q: What three things does a programme officer need from a review?
recall.a: The effect in absolute terms, how certain it is, and whether the evidence came from similar settings.

notes.2: Treat this as a route map. Slides 4 to 10 set the ground, 11 to 19 build the plan, and every later block follows the order a real review runs. If your question is about the shape of a field, read section 10 straight after section 1.
notes.4: Hold on to one idea: the unit of analysis is the study. A systematic review is research on research, so another team should be able to repeat your steps and land on the same set of studies. **Repeatability** is what separates it from an ordinary literature review.
notes.5: The three figures make one point: the primary literature has outgrown any single reader. They date from 2010 and the slide says they have only grown. When you pitch a review, **start with this problem**, then name who will use the answer.
notes.6: Notice the shape of both stories. One trial, or a set of early evaluations, produced a belief, and a review of the whole pile changed it. Ask of any claim which studies were in the **denominator** when people formed their view.
notes.7: Use this table as a menu. Match your question to the left column first, then check the time column against your deadline. The Borah figure at the foot is the sobering one: **67 weeks on average** from registration to publication, longer than most ranges above it.
notes.8: Test your own question with its verb. Words like reduces or increases point to a systematic review, 'what is known' points to scoping, and 'why' points to realist synthesis. Writing the question down first **saves you buying the wrong timeline**.
notes.9: Bookmark the 3ie portal and Campbell's development group for any South Asian question, then Cochrane when a health outcome is involved. The last line is a warning to you: **most reviews touching India are not Indian reviews**, so the local framing and search will be your contribution.
notes.10: The nine boxes are the workflow, and sections 2 to 9 walk through it in order. Section 10 is a separate toolkit, so keep it apart in your head. When you read someone else's review, you can **use the same boxes as a checklist**.
notes.12: Write each PICO element as a phrase you could hand to a screener. The comparison row matters most in development, since cash against nothing and cash against an unconditional transfer answer different questions. Adding the S for study design is where you **decide which designs count**.
notes.13: Run a one-day scoping search before you write anything. If you expect between roughly ten and a few hundred eligible studies, the question is workable. Use the slide's test for each criterion: **could a screener apply it without asking you?**
notes.14: Read this table row by row as a set of promises. The last column gives the reason for each exclusion, which is what you will later defend. The language row shows the cost of a careless default: **English-only screening** silently drops Indian-language evaluations.
notes.15: Use the list as a skeleton for your own protocol and tick each item as you write it. The subgroup point deserves a pause. Naming region, income level or design **before you see results** is what turns a subgroup finding into a test.
notes.16: File the protocol first, then search. A PROSPERO check can show that another team filed your question last year, and the time stamp lets readers compare your final methods with your plan. Outside health, **OSF Registries** gives you the same dated record for free.
notes.17: Count the people before you accept a deadline. Two screeners and extractors is a method requirement, and a librarian even for a day pays for itself. The slide's workaround for a doctoral student: **a supervisor screens a sample** and you report the disagreement rate.
notes.18: These are averages from 195 reviews, so yours may run shorter or longer. The time goes into screening, extraction and chasing grey literature, which is why development reviews sit at the slow end. If speed matters, **a rapid review** is honest provided you report its restrictions.
notes.19: Walk through this protocol as a template and compare each row with the earlier slides. Then find the real Campbell review and its protocol and read them side by side. The gap between plan and product shows you **how far a protocol constrains a review**.
notes.21: Pick sources by outcome and discipline, then add the field-specific ones. Remember Bramer's result: **no single database found every included study**, while four together reached 98 per cent. Plan at least three, and add Shodhganga and the 3ie portal for South Asia.
notes.22: Build the string concept by concept, with synonyms joined by OR inside a block and the blocks joined by AND. Leave the outcome block out when outcomes are named inconsistently. Then try five known studies: if one is missing, **the string needs fixing**.
notes.23: Controlled vocabulary catches what free text misses, so combine the two in every database that has a thesaurus. Copy the PubMed example's pattern of a Mesh term plus [tiab] synonyms. Each database needs its own **translated string**, and a person must correct the Polyglot draft.
notes.24: Most development evaluations sit on donor or NGO websites, so a journals-only search finds a biased subset. Use the list on the slide as your starting checklist and **log each site visit** as you go, because PRISMA-S asks for the site, date, terms and record count.
notes.25: Use this table to prove the evidence exists. The closing line separates thin indexing from thin evidence, and a regional review that skips these sources will wrongly report the second. Record **the retrieval date** for undated ministry PDFs.
notes.26: Run your main string in the databases first, then a simpler one in Scholar, screening the first 200 to 300 results and **reporting that cut-off**. Scholar is excellent for citation chasing and PDFs. Because results shift by day and by user, it cannot carry the review alone.
notes.27: Treat these five routes as one set. Each catches studies the others miss, and the slide says citation chasing alone often finds a fifth or more of the final set in development. Keep a count per route so your **flow diagram reports them separately**.
notes.28: Export in full, date-stamp, then deduplicate before anyone screens. The sample log entry is your model: database, date, string, limits, record count and file name. If you fill one in as you search, **the PRISMA numbers largely write themselves** later.
notes.30: Think of screening as two filters with different rules. At stage one the rule is when in doubt, keep, since a wrongly excluded study is gone for good. At stage two every exclusion needs **a reason from a fixed list**, and the counts per reason go in the report.
notes.31: Run the 100-record pilot before real screening and argue over every disagreement. Most conflicts expose a vague criterion, so reword it and log the amendment. Aim for a kappa above 0.6, and treat **a value below 0.4 as a stop sign** for the criteria.
notes.32: Choose the tool by budget. With no money, Rayyan's free tier gives you blinded dual screening, and its counts line up with PRISMA. Whatever you choose, switch on **blind mode** so neither screener sees the other's votes until conflicts are resolved.
notes.33: Machine help changes the order of the pile and leaves the decisions with people, who must still read every record shown. The unsolved part is when to stop. Pick a stopping rule, such as 50 irrelevant records in a row, and **write it into the methods**.
notes.34: Check the arithmetic yourself: 4,212 plus 318 minus 1,140 gives the 3,390 screened, then 3,390 minus 3,102 leaves 288 sought, and so on down. Remember the box counts **studies for the synthesis and reports for retrieval**, since one trial can have three papers.
notes.35: Work down the list from library access to free copies to the author's inbox. Keep a list of what you could not retrieve, because a reader may have access you lack. Do not drop a Bangla or Tamil study by default: **language exclusion is a decision to justify**.
notes.36: Do the sums before you promise a date: 5,000 records at 60 to 100 an hour is 50 to 80 hours per screener, then 300 full texts at 30 to 60 minutes each. Savings come from a tighter search, and **the second screener stays**.
notes.38: Write the form from the protocol before you read a paper, because a missing field sends you back through every paper already done. Pilot it on five studies with two extractors. Keep the **raw extraction separate from the analysis table**.
notes.39: Scan the left column as a checklist and mark any group your form lacks. The forgotten rows are the comparator, the unit of assignment and the timepoints. In the microfinance example, **what the control group could borrow** changes what the intervention means.
notes.40: Use this table when a paper reports the wrong statistic. Each row shows what you hold, what you need and the route between them. Write down **which conversion you used for every number**, since two teams can pool the same studies and disagree because they converted differently.
notes.41: The three figures argue for double extraction: a fifth more errors with one person, bought with a third less time. If the team is tiny, the compromise is one extractor and a second who **verifies every number against the paper**. Settle disagreements by returning to the paper and never by averaging.
notes.42: Each of these three cases hides a trap: a shared control group counted twice, three papers counted as three studies, and village-level randomisation analysed as though people were independent. Choose your rule, apply it every time and **write it into the methods**.
notes.43: Follow the order ask, derive, impute. Ask for the specific number, name the table, and set a three-week deadline. If you impute, run the analysis with and without those studies. Never read a missing result as zero, because **missing data is itself a bias signal**.
notes.45: Appraisal asks whether a study's design could have produced a systematic error, so a large, well-published trial can still be high risk. Judge each outcome separately and judge each area on its own, **never with a summed score**, as Cochrane advises.
notes.46: Keep the five RoB 2 questions in order: how people were assigned, what happened to them afterwards, who dropped out, how the outcome was measured, and what was reported. The overall judgement is the **worst of the five**, so one high-risk area makes the outcome high.
notes.47: ROBINS-I starts with confounding because that is where non-randomised studies usually fall short. Write into the protocol which confounders a credible study must handle. For a cash-transfer review the slide lists baseline income, household size and **programme targeting rules**.
notes.48: Match the appraisal to the identifying assumption of each design: parallel trends for DiD, common support for matching, the exclusion restriction for IV, and manipulation of the running variable for RDD. Record that assumption in the extraction form, since it **decides the weight** a study deserves.
notes.49: Pick the tool by design and use one tool per design. Note the warning on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, which the slide says has poor inter-rater reliability. Finally, use the results: an appraisal that never changes the synthesis is **decoration**.
notes.50: Franco's numbers make the file drawer visible: 10 of 48 null studies published against 56 of 91 strong ones. Prevention comes first, meaning searches of registries and theses. Detection tools need at least ten studies, so **skip the funnel test on a handful**.
notes.51: Read the funnel plot by looking for an empty bottom-left corner. Then hold two readings in mind: publication bias, or real heterogeneity, as with pilots in favourable sites against government-scale trials. Whichever you favour, **say so and show your reasoning**.
notes.52: Check your review against these four places and see whether the risk-of-bias judgement shows up in each. Then write the sentence the slide suggests, comparing the pooled effect for low-risk studies with all studies. If you cannot write it, **the appraisal was not used**.
notes.54: Meta-analysis is a weighted average where precision sets the weight, and the arithmetic is short. The judgement lies in whether studies ask the same question of comparable populations against a comparable comparator. **The protocol defines the fruit**, so decide what is combinable before you see results.
notes.55: Pick the measure from the outcome type, then read the watch-for column. Two traps: odds ratios overstate risk ratios when events are common, and ratios are pooled on the log scale. Kraft also argues that Cohen's benchmarks are **too demanding for field programmes**.
notes.56: Work this table with a calculator. Weight is one over the squared standard error, so study C's SE of 0.05 gives 400 and three-quarters of the share. The lesson is that **precision decides influence**, and a big effect with a wide error barely moves the pooled estimate.
notes.57: Read Q, I² and τ² as three different things. Q is a test, I² is a proportion beyond chance, and τ² is the amount in effect-size units. Report all three plus the prediction interval, because **I² climbs with study precision** even when the disagreement stays the same.
notes.58: Compare the two models' numbers: fixed effect gave 0.093 with an interval above zero, random effects gave 0.134 with an interval spanning zero. Adding τ² flattens the weights and widens the interval. Choose the model **in the protocol**, before the data arrive.
notes.59: Read a forest plot with the five questions on the slide. The diamond summarises the rows and cannot replace them. Watch for **two clusters on opposite sides** of the line of no effect, a picture that says the studies should not have been pooled.
notes.60: Name your subgroups in the protocol and keep them few. Test the difference between subgroups, and ignore whether each one is significant alone. With 15 studies the slide allows one moderator in meta-regression, so use **ten studies per moderator** as your working rule.
notes.61: Count studies and effect sizes separately, always. Pick a rule such as primary outcome or longest follow-up, average within a study, or use RVE, which corrects standard errors for clustering within studies. Whichever you choose, **state the rule and both counts** wherever a k appears.
notes.62: Run the whole table, including checks that turn out inconvenient. Leave-one-out is the quickest: re-run k times and name any study whose removal changes the conclusion. Reporting **only the supportive checks** is the selective reporting a review exists to catch.
notes.63: Choose R or Jamovi if you work on an old laptop with no budget. Both are free, both run offline, and a Jamovi analysis can be reproduced in R. Put the extraction sheet and the script in a **public repository** so anyone can rerun the review.
notes.65: Decide before you start what you will do when pooling fails, and cite SWiM. Group studies by a stated logic, standardise effects even when you cannot pool them, and count with denominators. Guard against **a narrative review in disguise**, a paragraph per study with no conclusion they support.
notes.66: Count directions, since underpowered studies make a true small effect look like a failure when you count significance. Nine of ten positive gives p = 0.02, and six of ten gives 0.75. Direction counting says whether an effect exists and **never how big it is**.
notes.67: Choose the method from the question: experience and barriers suggest thematic synthesis, a commissioner's framework suggests framework synthesis, and interpretive depth suggests meta-ethnography. Whatever you pick, rate confidence with CERQual. Two thin studies from one district give **low confidence** however vivid the quotes.
notes.68: Use the four steps as a plan. A realist review tracks the reasoning of the people a programme reaches, so a mechanism fires only where cash was the constraint. Do not commission one if you want an effect size. It **pairs well with a meta-analysis**.
notes.69: Pick the simplest design that fits your team. The segregated design with a matrix is the common one, and the matrix is the useful table, with components in rows and trials in columns. Keep the two appraisals **separate** and budget for two skill sets.
notes.70: Choose a scoping review when the question concerns the shape of a literature, and keep the rigorous search. The gap map is the product a funder can read in ten minutes. **Blank cells are the point**, so make each gap specific enough to commission.
notes.71: Evans and Popova show why six reviews of one question can disagree: only 3 of 227 studies sat in all six. Before you start, compare existing reviews' inclusion criteria with yours, and use a published taxonomy so categories can be compared. Once harmonised, the reviews **agreed on more**.
notes.73: GRADE answers how far to trust each pooled number, outcome by outcome. Start randomised evidence at high and observational evidence at low, then move down for five reasons and up for three. The product is **a sentence a minister can read**, with the certainty word in it.
notes.74: Use the table to justify every downgrade in writing. Each of the five reasons costs one level or two, so randomised evidence with two serious problems ends at low. Apply identical rules to outcomes you like and outcomes you dislike, and **give the reason beside each cell**.
notes.75: Look at how the table pairs a relative effect with an absolute one at a stated baseline. An RR of 1.08 means 6 more per 100 when 75 per 100 enrol. Put the **certainty rating beside each outcome** and keep the table to about seven outcomes.
notes.76: Use the checklist as an audit of your own draft: any item with no page number is a gap. Items 7 and 27 catch many teams, since they want the full search strategy verbatim and a public home for the extraction sheet and code. **Pick the extension** that fits your design.
notes.77: Write the five paragraphs in order and keep limits of the evidence apart from limits of the review. The applicability paragraph is the one South Asian readers need: name the studies from comparable settings. Replace 'more research is needed' with **a specific, fundable study**.
notes.78: Match the outlet to your question before you write. Health outcomes lead to Cochrane, social welfare and development to Campbell or 3ie, and general development journals expect more than a summary. Publish the protocol first, since that separates your work from **a literature review with a flow diagram**.
notes.79: Put the search date on the first page and plan the update from the start. The slide gives about five and a half years as the median before a review needs updating. A living review needs a budget line, because **an unfunded living review is a stale one** with a misleading label.
notes.81: Keep the distinction sharp: a systematic review reads 40 studies closely, while a bibliometric analysis counts 4,000 and reads none. Use bibliometrics for questions about the field itself. Do not claim a programme works from citation counts, because **attention is not evidence**.
notes.82: Use one technique from each family. Counts tell you who and where. Co-citation shows the intellectual base and bibliographic coupling shows the current research front, so **co-citation looks back and coupling looks at the present**. State the database and date, and name every cluster.
notes.83: Pick the source before the query, because the source decides who is missing. Scopus and Web of Science under-represent social sciences and non-English journals, so a South Asian study should add OpenAlex or Dimensions. Record **which database each number came from**.
notes.84: Plan for cleaning to take half your time. Author-name variants, institution spellings and keyword forms all need merging, and the tools do it badly. Keep a **thesaurus file** and cite it, and report record counts at each cleaning step so the analysis can be rerun.
notes.85: Start with the easy path on the slide: export from Scopus or OpenAlex, run descriptives in biblioshiny, draw the maps in VOSviewer. Save the map and network files with the export so a reader can reopen **exactly the figure in your paper**.
notes.86: Treat the map as evidence and the caption as the analysis. Node size, distance and colour each mean one thing, and the resolution setting changes the number of clusters, so report it. Name each cluster by reading two or three central works and **say how you chose the label**.
notes.87: Match each indicator to its proper use and read the misuse column twice. The h-index rewards volume, an impact factor describes a journal and says little about one article, and altmetrics measure attention. The Leiden Manifesto gives the working rule: **numbers support expert judgement**.
notes.88: Report each law together with the sentence that says what follows from it. Bradford's core tells a reviewer where to hand-search, and Lotka's curve tells a funder how many sustained researchers exist. A number with no consequence is **filler**.
notes.89: Read the table as a template for writing: step, decision, number, interpretation. The numbers are invented for teaching. Then read the closing sentence on what the study cannot say, and **write the same kind of limit into your own paper**.
notes.90: Report output and uptake separately, and name the database for each number. Check journals against DOAJ and the other tests before you count them, or you report predatory output as achievement. A Scopus-only map shows **the part of the field that faces outward**.
notes.91: Write the question first, one that counts and maps can answer. Use the five-step structure, name clusters from reading, and finish with the 'so what'. Reviewers reject default figures and a conclusion that the field is growing. **Pairing it with another product** makes the numbers matter.
notes.93: Treat this table as a shopping list with one free tool for each stage. Save every search strategy as run, keep a 'source page' column in extraction, and keep scripts public. Slide 10 promised that nothing here needs a licence, and **this stack is how**.
notes.94: Use the table to turn a deadline into a staffing plan. The 26 to 46 weeks of effort fits Borah's 67 weeks elapsed. Protect the librarian and the second screener, since those are the two roles you cannot recover later. A rapid review compresses the plan to **8 to 12 weeks**.
notes.95: Use AI as a third pair of eyes whose accuracy you have measured. For screening, test sensitivity on a sample humans already screened, since below about 95% it cannot exclude anything. A discovery tool as your only search fails PRISMA item 7. **Report tool, version, date, prompt and checks**.
notes.96: Scan the twelve rows against your protocol and mark any you are close to. The prevention column holds the numbers worth remembering: ten studies before a funnel test, one effect per study, three or more databases. Each prevention is **a decision you can write down**.
notes.97: Read a review in the order of the six boxes. Registration comes first because a missing protocol sinks the rest, and certainty comes last because the abstract's verbs should match it. A programme officer needs **the absolute effect, how certain it is, and whether the settings match**.
notes.98: Pick one handbook and one book for your discipline. The Cochrane Handbook chapters named on the slide (5, 6, 8, 10 and 13) are the core. For a development focus add the **Campbell and 3ie methods guides**, and the ImpactMojo courses that cover the primary studies.
notes.99: Use this page as a final audit: for each line, can you point to the place in your own review? The last two lines matter most for South Asia, the applicability paragraph and the closing sentence that **every decision can be defended in writing**.
